chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman, the freedman of Tirbal, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

Regarding a man who had intercourse with his slave-girl, and that he used to send her on his errands, and that she became pregnant, and that news reached him of her having a defect, Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: "When she gives birth, he keeps the child and does not sell him, and assigns him a share in his house."

He said: Then it was said to him, "A man who has intercourse with his slave-girl, and that he did not use to send her on his errands, and that he suspected her (of infidelity), and she became pregnant." He said: "When she gives birth, he keeps the child and does not sell him, and assigns him a share from his house and his wealth, and this case is not like that one."
ai.seo_question: What is the difference in legal ruling for a child born to a slave-girl when the master sends her on errands versus when he suspects her of infidelity?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of *luluq* (linking lineage) by distinguishing between a slave-girl who is frequently sent on errands, implying exclusive access and thus legitimate offspring, and one where suspicion of infidelity exists. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while the child is retained and not sold in both cases, the financial provision (*nafaqah*) and inheritance share (*nasib*) are adjusted based on the degree of certainty regarding the master's exclusive access, reflecting the principle that lineage follows the one with whom she is most likely to have been intimate.
